title: SpaceX Starship Flight 13 Targets Friday Launch After Engine Abort and Weather Delays
excerpt: The 400-foot rocket will attempt its second V3 test from Texas, deploying 20 live Starlink satellites and testing heat shield cameras.
body:
• SpaceX is targeting July 25 for Starship Flight 13 after a July 16 engine abort and weather postponements due to Tropical Storm Bertha
  • The mission will deploy 20 live V3 Starlink satellites for the first time, with six equipped with cameras to photograph the ship’s heat shield
  • Key objectives include a controlled booster landing, single-engine relight, and ship splashdown in the Indian Ocean
  • Success is critical for NASA’s Artemis moon landing program and SpaceX’s planned Florida launches

SpaceX is preparing for yet another launch attempt of its Starship Flight 13, the second test of the upgraded Version 3 rocket, after a string of setbacks pushed the mission from mid-July into late July.

The 400-foot rocket — the largest and most powerful ever built — is now targeting Friday, July 25, for liftoff from SpaceX’s Starbase facility in Boca Chica, Texas, with a 90-minute launch window opening at 5:45 p.m. CT. The delay from the original July 24 target came after Tropical Storm Bertha brought poor visibility conditions.

A Troubled Path to the Pad

Flight 13 was originally scheduled for July 16, but SpaceX experienced a rare post-ignition abort when multiple engines on the Super Heavy booster failed to ignite during the countdown’s final moments. CEO Elon Musk confirmed that several engines were replaced during the subsequent week of repairs.

https://x.com/SpaceX/status/2080384481043656948

A July 23 attempt was then scrubbed due to weather concerns as Tropical Storm Bertha battered the Texas Gulf Coast. SpaceX explained that clear skies are essential for ground-based cameras to capture footage of Starship’s heat shield during ascent — a primary data-gathering objective for the flight.

What’s Different This Time

Flight 13 marks the second outing for the V3 configuration. The mission will carry 20 live V3 Starlink satellites instead of the 22 simulators flown previously. This will be the first time SpaceX flies the upgraded V3 Starlink configuration to space aboard Starship.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Ew0Xu1RT8oc

Once deployed, the satellites will extend solar arrays and antennas, then attempt to connect to the existing Starlink network using high-capacity laser links. The satellites are test articles only — they will reenter the atmosphere and burn up about 20 minutes after deployment.

Six of the 20 satellites are equipped with cameras specifically designed to photograph Starship’s heat shield tiles during flight, giving engineers critical data on thermal protection performance ahead of planned booster return-to-launch-site missions.

Stakes for NASA and Space Watchers

The mission’s other objectives include a controlled booster descent (though not a tower catch this time), a single-engine relight in space, and a ship splashdown in the Indian Ocean. Each successful test brings SpaceX closer to having Starship certified for NASA’s Artemis program, which plans to use the vehicle as a lunar lander for astronaut missions to the Moon.

SpaceX has also stated that the first Starship launch from Kennedy Space Center’s Pad 39A in Florida could happen by the end of the year. For India’s growing space community — which has tracked ISRO’s own reusable launch vehicle program with keen interest — Starship’s V3 milestones offer a benchmark for the next generation of heavy-lift rockets.

What to Watch

SpaceX will livestream the approximately one-hour mission beginning about 30 minutes before liftoff on its website and X account. Weather remains the primary variable; forecasters are monitoring residual effects from Bertha along the Texas coast.
